Provide for each combination three real-world systems. So we need to list CA, CP, AP each with three examples. Provide maybe a table. Also discuss the trade-offs, what each combination means, how real systems choose. Provide formal definition: a distributed data store can at most guarantee two of the three properties: Consistency, Availability, Partition tolerance. Provide definitions: C: all nodes see the same data at same time. A: every request receives a response. P: system continues to operate despite network partitions. Formal: a system is called "C" if it satisfies atomic (linearizable) reads/writes; "A" if it satisfies liveness; "P" if it can tolerate arbitrarily many messages lost/delayed. Then CAP theorem: it's impossible for a distributed system to simultaneously guarantee all three. Provide proof sketch: assume a system that is consistent and available in presence of partition; then you can cause a split-brain scenario leading to inconsistency. Provide references.

We need to be careful to not violate policy. It's allowed. Provide examples: CA: Traditional relational databases with synchronous replication (e.g., PostgreSQL with synchronous replication in a single data center, but not partition tolerant; if network partition occurs, they may become unavailable). Or maybe some cluster that chooses consistency and availability but not partition tolerance: e.g., single-node databases, two-phase commit based systems like traditional RDBMS (MySQL Cluster?). But CAP theorem applies only in presence of partitions; CA systems sacrifice partition tolerance, thus they are not tolerant of network partitions; they become unavailable or inconsistent when partition occurs. Real-world CA examples: Traditional RDBMS like Oracle, MySQL with synchronous replication (if network partition, one side may become unavailable). So they are typically single-node systems or systems that assume no network partitions (e.g., within a single data center).
